Generalized additive models for location, scale, and shape can be estimated by
penalized likelihood or by Bayesian sampling. In `gamlss2`, Bayesian estimation
uses the same distributional formulas, family objects, and smooth terms as the
usual fitting functions. The sampler follows the Bayesian additive model
framework described by @bamlss2018.

There are two ways to run the sampler. The function `bamlss2()` fits a
model directly by Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), whereas `mcmc()` starts from an already fitted
`gamlss2` model. This vignette illustrates both workflows and shows how to
inspect posterior effects, samples, and predictions.

The fitting notation is introduced in [First Steps](firststeps.html).
[Prediction and Uncertainty](prediction.html) uses the same ozone formula and
Gamma parameterization for likelihood-based inference, with a training/test
split. Here we use all complete observations to illustrate posterior inference.

## Data and model

We use the `airquality` data and model daily ozone concentration. Ozone is
positive and right-skewed, so a Gamma distribution is a useful starting point.
We model the conditional mean (`mu`) with smooth effects of temperature
and wind speed. The conditional coefficient of variation (`sigma`) varies
smoothly with temperature.

```{r}
#| message: false
library("gamlss2")

air <- subset(airquality, !is.na(Ozone))
```

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Daily ozone concentration and temperature in the airquality data."
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot of daily ozone against temperature, with higher ozone concentrations on hotter days."
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(Ozone ~ Temp, data = air,
  pch = 16, col = adjustcolor(1, 0.3),
  xlab = "Temperature (°F)", ylab = "Ozone (ppb)")
```

The distributional formula is

```{r}
f <- Ozone ~ s(Temp) + s(Wind) | s(Temp)
```

The first right-hand side specifies the predictor for `mu`; the second specifies
the predictor for `sigma`. The same formula can therefore be used for
likelihood-based and Bayesian estimation.

## Bayesian estimation

The convenience function `bamlss2()` sets up the model and runs the Bayesian
sampler. By default, a small number of backfitting iterations is performed
first to obtain starting values before MCMC sampling begins.

```{r}
set.seed(1328)
m <- bamlss2(
  f,
  data = air,
  family = GA,
  n.iter = 1200,
  burnin = 200,
  thin = 1,
  trace = FALSE
)
```

The returned object inherits from class `gamlss2`, so the usual extractor and
plotting methods remain available. In addition, it contains the retained MCMC
samples.

```{r}
summary(m)
```

The sampler uses block Metropolis-Hastings updates for linear and smooth
coefficients. Smooth terms are updated using penalized weighted least squares
proposals, while smoothing variances are sampled by inverse Gamma or slice sampling.
See `?BS` for details of the sampler.

## Posterior effects

Calling `plot()` displays the fitted additive effects. For a Bayesian fit these
are obtained from the posterior samples stored in the fitted object.

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Posterior smooth effects for the Gamma mean and coefficient of variation."
#| fig-alt: "Three panels showing temperature and wind effects on the mean and a temperature effect on the coefficient of variation."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.5
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1), cex = 1)
plot(m, spar = FALSE)
par(op)
```

The MCMC draws are available in the `samples` component. For example, the
intercept draws for the distribution parameters can be inspected directly.

```{r}
cn <- grep("(Intercept)", colnames(m$samples),
  fixed = TRUE, value = TRUE)
head(m$samples[, cn, drop = FALSE])
```

## MCMC diagnostics

Posterior summaries are only useful if the sampler has explored the relevant
part of the parameter space adequately. Trace plots and autocorrelation plots
can be obtained with `which = "samples"`. Here we inspect the intercept in the
`mu` model.

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Trace and autocorrelation of the intercept draws for the Gamma mean."
#| fig-alt: "Intercept draws in sampling order alongside their autocorrelation at lags up to 60."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1), cex = 1)
plot(m, which = "samples", parameter = "mu",
  terms = "(Intercept)", lag.max = 60, spar = FALSE)
par(op)
```

The `parameter` and `terms` arguments can be used to select other coefficients.
Smooth terms contain several basis coefficients, so inspecting a smooth can
produce several trace and autocorrelation plots.

This short run illustrates the workflow. In an analysis, inspect draws for
several coefficients and compare chains started from different values. Slow
decay in the autocorrelation plot means successive draws carry similar
information, so a longer run may be needed for precise posterior summaries.

Sampling can be extended by calling `mcmc()` again on the fitted object. The
existing draws are retained and the newly retained draws are appended to
`samples`, so the call can be repeated as necessary. The `burnin` argument
applies to each additional run.

```{r}
#| eval: false
m <- mcmc(m,
  n.iter = 1200,
  burnin = 200,
  thin = 1,
  trace = FALSE
)
```

## Posterior predictions

For an object returned by `bamlss2()`, `predict()` uses the stored posterior
samples. Supplying `FUN` selects how they are summarized. We evaluate the model
over the observed temperature range and keep wind speed fixed at its median.

```{r}
nd <- data.frame(
  Temp = seq(min(air$Temp), max(air$Temp), length.out = 100),
  Wind = median(air$Wind)
)

post_interval <- function(x) {
  q <- quantile(x, probs = c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975), na.rm = TRUE)
  setNames(q, c("lower", "fit", "upper"))
}

pmu <- predict(m, newdata = nd, parameter = "mu",
  FUN = post_interval)
psigma <- predict(m, newdata = nd, parameter = "sigma",
  FUN = post_interval)

head(pmu)
```

The resulting intervals are 95% pointwise credible intervals for the
distribution parameters; `fit` is the posterior median. They are not prediction
intervals for a future ozone observation or simultaneous bands for a whole
curve. Wind speed is held fixed, while the displayed observations include all
wind speeds.

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Posterior medians and 95% pointwise credible intervals for the Gamma mean and coefficient of variation, at median wind speed."
#| fig-alt: "Median curves with shaded credible intervals across temperature. Observed ozone values are overlaid in the mean panel."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1), cex = 1)

plot(Ozone ~ Temp, data = air,
  pch = 16, col = adjustcolor(1, 0.2),
  xlab = "Temperature (°F)", ylab = "Mean ozone (ppb)")
polygon(c(nd$Temp, rev(nd$Temp)),
  c(pmu$lower, rev(pmu$upper)),
  border = NA, col = adjustcolor(4, 0.15))
lines(nd$Temp, pmu$fit, col = 4, lwd = 2)

plot(nd$Temp, psigma$fit, type = "n",
  ylim = range(psigma[, c("lower", "upper")]),
  xlab = "Temperature (°F)", ylab = expression("Coefficient of variation " * sigma))
polygon(c(nd$Temp, rev(nd$Temp)),
  c(psigma$lower, rev(psigma$upper)),
  border = NA, col = adjustcolor(4, 0.15))
lines(nd$Temp, psigma$fit, col = 4, lwd = 2)

par(op)
```

Other posterior summaries can be obtained by changing `FUN`. For example,
posterior means and standard deviations are returned with

```{r}
head(predict(m, newdata = nd, type = "parameter", FUN = mean))
head(predict(m, newdata = nd, type = "parameter", FUN = sd))
```

For a quantity that depends on several parameters, retain the joint draws with
`predict(m, newdata = nd, FUN = identity)`, compute the quantity for each draw,
and then summarize. [Prediction and Uncertainty](prediction.html#including-coefficient-uncertainty)
also shows how to generate future responses from these distributions. Using
posterior draws in that construction gives posterior predictive intervals.

## Starting from a fitted `gamlss2` model

Bayesian sampling can also be started from an existing likelihood-based fit.
This is useful when a model has already been developed with `gamlss2()` and the
same specification should subsequently be sampled. The function `mcmc()` uses the
fitted coefficients and smoothing parameters as starting values and merges the
posterior output back into the model object.

```{r}
m <- gamlss2(f, data = air, family = GA, trace = FALSE)
```

The corresponding MCMC fit is obtained with

```{r}
#| eval: false
set.seed(1328)
m2 <- mcmc(m,
  n.iter = 1200,
  burnin = 200,
  thin = 1,
  trace = FALSE
)
```

Once fitted, `m2` supports the same posterior summaries and plots as the object
returned by `bamlss2()`.

The fitted model supplied to `mcmc()` must retain the design information needed
by the sampler. In particular, reduced model objects that discard this
information cannot be used to restart sampling.

The general GAMLSS formulation is described in @Rigby+Stasinopoulos:2005. For
the Bayesian additive distributional framework and the MCMC methodology, see
@bamlss2018.
